entries.meaning: Guha continued: “I was deceitful, cowardly, ill-minded, and low-born, outside worldly and Vedic convention in every way; from the moment Rāma made me his own, I became an ornament of the worlds.” Seeing his love and hearing his lovely petition, Bharata’s younger brother also embraced him. Announcing his name in gracious words, the Niṣāda respectfully saluted all the queens. Knowing him equal to Lakṣmaṇa, they blessed him: “Live happily for a hundred thousand years.” Seeing the Niṣāda, the city’s women and men became as happy as though they beheld Lakṣmaṇa. They said, “This life has gained its reward: Rāmabhadra embraced him with full arms.” Hearing them extol his fortune, the Niṣāda joyfully led the party onward. All his servants, alerted to their master’s disposition, went out and made lodgings at houses, under trees, beside lakes, in gardens, and in the woods.

When Bharata saw Śṛṅgaverapura, affection loosened every limb. Supported by the Niṣāda, he looked like humility and love embodied. In this way Bharata, with army and whole company, went and beheld the world-purifying Gaṅgā. He bowed toward Rāma’s landing place, and his mind became so absorbed that it seemed he had met Rāma. The city’s men and women bowed, joyfully beholding the water suffused with Brahman. They bathed, then joined their hands and prayed for an abundant love of Rāmacandra’s feet. Bharata said: “Gaṅgā, your dust is a wish-fulfilling cow giving every joy to a servant. Joining my hands, I ask this one boon: an innate love for Sītā and Rāma’s feet.” Having bathed in this way upon the guru’s instruction, Bharata learned that the mothers too had bathed and led everyone to camp.

People established camps here and there, and Bharata inquired after the condition of everyone. After worshiping the gods and receiving permission, the two brothers went to Rāma’s mothers. Pressing their feet and repeatedly speaking tenderly, Bharata honored each mother. Entrusting their service to his brother, he called the Niṣāda to himself. Hand clasped in his friend’s hand, he set out, body slack with abundant love. He asked: “Friend, show me that place; let me cool for a little while the burning of eyes and mind—the place where Sītā, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa slept that night.” As he spoke, both eyes filled with water. Hearing Bharata, the Niṣāda grieved and immediately led him there. Beneath the sacred śiṃśapā tree where Raghubara had rested, Bharata prostrated with profound love and reverence.

Seeing the lovely bed of kuśa grass, Bharata bowed and walked around it in reverence. He touched to his eyes the dust marked by their feet; the fullness of his love cannot be expressed. He saw two or four golden specks and placed them upon his head, regarding them as Sītā herself. With tearful eyes and shame in his heart he spoke gracious words to his friend: “Sītā, robbed of splendor and bereft of radiance, lay here as Ayodhyā’s women and men lie overwhelmed. To whom can I compare her father, King Janaka, for whom all the world’s enjoyments lie within his palm? Her father-in-law is the sun of the solar dynasty, a king envied by Indra, lord of Amarāvatī. Her life’s lord is sovereign Raghunātha; whoever becomes great does so through Rāma’s greatness. Seeing the bed of Sītā—the jewel among faithful wives, whose husband is her deity—why did my heart not split? It is harder by far than even the thunderbolt.”

“Lakṣmaṇa, the charming younger one fit to be cherished, has never had and never will have a brother equal to him. Beloved to citizens and cherished by father and mothers, he is dearer than life to Sītā and Raghubara. His form is tender and his nature delicate; father would not allow even the wind to touch his body. Yet he endures every kind of hardship in the forest—this chest of mine has put millions of thunderbolts to shame. Rāma took birth and illuminated the world, an ocean of beauty, character, happiness, and every virtue. His nature gives joy to citizens, relatives, guru, father, and mothers alike. Even enemies praise Rāma; his speech, manner of meeting, and humility captivate the mind. A hundred million Sarasvatīs and a hundred million Śeṣas could not enumerate the Lord’s host of virtues. Yet Rāma, jewel of Raghu’s line, embodiment of happiness and treasury of blessing and joy, slept upon a bed of kuśa grass on the ground—Fate’s course is immensely strong.”

“No one ever let even the sound of suffering reach Rāma’s ears. The king protected him as one tends the tree of life; all the mothers guarded him day and night as eyelids guard eyes or a serpent its jewel. He now wanders the forest on foot and lives upon tubers, roots, fruits, and flowers. Shame upon Kaikeyī, root of misfortune, who turned against one dearer than life. Shame again upon me, unfortunate ocean of sin, for whose sake every upheaval occurred. Fate created me a stain upon the lineage, and my mother made me a traitor to my master.” Hearing him, the Niṣāda lovingly consoled him: “Lord, why grieve in vain? Rāma is dear to you and you are dear to Rāma; you are innocent—the fault belongs to hostile Fate.”

Hearing his friend’s words, Bharata held courage in his heart and returned to camp remembering Raghubīra. Receiving the news, the city’s anguished women and men went to see the place. They circumambulated it, bowed, and heaped limitless blame upon Kaikeyī. Taking eye after eye full of tears, they blamed perverse Fate. Some praised Bharata’s affection; others said the king had fulfilled love. They condemned themselves and praised the Niṣāda—who could express such bewilderment and grief? All the people remained awake through the night in this way. At daybreak the boatmen set to work. Guha reported to the guru, arrayed the handsome boats, and bowed them into service; all the mothers boarded new boats. Within four watches everyone had crossed. Bharata then landed and attended to all. After morning rites, he bowed at the mothers’ feet and the guru’s head, placed the Niṣāda companies in front, and set the army moving.

The Niṣāda lord led the way, and all the mothers’ palanquins moved. Bharata summoned his younger brother and placed him with them; the guru traveled with the brahmins. Bharata himself bowed to the Gaṅgā and remembered Rāma with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. He set out on foot, while grooms led his horses alongside by the reins. Good servants repeatedly begged, “Lord, please mount a horse.” Bharata replied, “Rāma went forward on this road on foot; for whom, then, were chariots, elephants, and horses made? It would be proper for me to go upon my head, for a servant’s duty is harsher than every other.” Seeing Bharata’s conduct and hearing his tender words, all the servants’ companies reproached themselves in shame. By the third watch Bharata entered Prayāga, crying “Rāma, Sītā! Rāma, Sītā!” as love surged again and again.

How did the blisters glisten upon Bharata’s feet? Like drops of dew upon closed lotus buds. The whole company was saddened to hear that Bharata had arrived that day on foot. After checking that everyone had bathed, they came and bowed to the Triveṇī. They bathed by full rite in the mingled pale and dark waters, gave gifts, and honored brahmins. Seeing the dark and white waves, Bharata’s body thrilled and he joined his hands: “King of sacred fords, giver of every desire, your majesty is known to the Vedas and manifest throughout the world. I beg alms after abandoning my own proper aim—for what wrong act will a distressed person not do? Knowing this inwardly, wise and generous one, you make a petitioner’s words fruitful in the world. I have no taste for wealth, duty, or pleasure and desire no destination of liberation. Birth after birth, let me love Rāma’s feet; I ask no other boon.”

Bharata prayed: “Though Rāma know me as crooked and the world call me traitor to guru and master, by your favor let my love for Sītā and Rāma’s feet increase day by day. A cātaka may remember nothing else its whole life while the cloud forgets it, and though it begs for water the cloud may cast lightning, hail, and stones. The cātaka’s cry may grow faint and its body waste away, yet its love grows and all is well. Just as gold acquires greater luster when burned, so may my vow toward my beloved’s feet endure.” Hearing Bharata’s words, a gentle voice arose from the midst of the Triveṇī, granting blessing: “Dear Bharata, you are holy in every way and your devotion to Rāma’s feet is fathomless. Do not harbor fruitless shame in your mind; no one is as dear to Rāma as you.” Hearing the river’s favorable words, Bharata’s body thrilled and his heart rejoiced; declaring Bharata blessed, the delighted gods showered flowers.
